chunks.text: Dispatch · July 16, twenty twenty-six · 15 min read · By Don Goldstein

+3.4% against 42%. Restaurant menu prices rose 3.4% over the year to June twenty twenty-six, the tamest inflation in years, yet 42% of operators still closed last year without a profit. The gap between those two numbers is five cost fronts, moving on five different clocks under one calm average.
In short

The headline is calm: restaurant menu prices rose 3.4% over the year to June twenty twenty-six (full-service 3.7%, fast food 3.1%), the tamest menu inflation in years, yet 42% of operators finished last year with no profit.

The average hides the movers. Retail beef ran 12.9% year-on-year and coffee peaked near 18.5% in April before cooling. Nine in ten operators name food, labor, insurance, energy and swipe fees as significant challenges at once.

Beef is the one structural front: the US cattle herd is the smallest since 1951, and Usda forecasts twenty twenty-six beef and veal up about 7.5%, with the price peak likely in twenty twenty-seven. Reprice it deliberately, not seasonally.

Some fronts are easing: coffee cooled 2.0% month-on-month in June, the Brazil tariff on coffee and beef came off in November twenty twenty-five, a 38 dollars billion swipe-fee settlement trims interchange, and property-insurance rates are softening.

Card fees are the quiet third-largest line: US merchants paid a record 198.25 dollars billion in swipe fees in twenty twenty-five, up more than 80% since the pandemic. Read your own invoices against the Cost Index and plate-cost, not the headline.
Why restaurant costs feel worse than the 3.4% number.

I keep the order guide on a clipboard by the walk-in, and in June the number that stopped me wasn’t the beef. It was a case of to-go lids, up a few cents each, quiet, easy to sign for without looking. The beef I had priced in months ago. The lids I hadn’t, and a few cents on every order that leaves the building is real money by Sunday. If you run a floor, you know that feeling in your stomach when a line you weren’t watching moves. You already price your proteins and watch your food cost every week; the lines that hurt in twenty twenty-six are the ones nobody told you to watch.

Here are two numbers that are both true, and the space between them is the whole dispatch. Restaurant menu prices rose 3.4% over the year to June twenty twenty-six, the tamest menu inflation in years. And 42% of operators closed last year without a profit. The average is calm. The floor is not.
The average is the tamest it has been in years. The spread is the widest I have paid.

I’m not here to tell you costs are exploding, because the data and my own invoices disagree with that story. Food away from home, the government’s name for a restaurant meal, rose 3.4% over the year to June twenty twenty-six, with full-service at 3.7% and fast food at 3.1%. That is a blended figure, one line drawn across every restaurant in the country. It gives you the temperature of the room and nothing about the fire in the corner.

The counterweight sits right next to it. In the National Restaurant Association’s twenty twenty-six read, 42% of operators said their restaurant wasn’t profitable last year, and about 60% said traffic got softer even as their sales dollars grew. Checks up, guests down. More than seven in ten diners say they’d eat out more if they had more money to spend. Right now the revenue is carried by higher prices, not more covers, and that is a fragile way to carry it.
Underneath the average, the menu splits into fronts moving on their own clocks. This is the chart that should reset the panic in either direction.

A bar chart showing the twelve-month price move for several restaurant cost lines, to make the point that the average sits on top of a much wider spread. Restaurant menus overall rose three point four percent, full-service menus three point seven, and grocery is forecast up two point eight. Underneath that calm average, retail beef ran twelve point nine percent over the year, and coffee peaked at eighteen point five percent year-on-year in April before cooling to a two point nine percent beverage reading by June. The two loudest lines under the headline move roughly four to five times faster than the menu average that is supposed to cover them.

An average is a compromise. It smooths five very different pressures into one polite figure, and the smoothing is exactly what hides the pain. Usda’s outlook for the year has restaurant prices rising 3.6% against grocery’s 2.8%, eating out getting more expensive faster than eating in, which your guest feels at the table every time. More than nine in ten operators name food, labor, insurance, energy and card fees as significant challenges, all at once. The industry is still projected to ring up a record 1.55 dollars trillion in sales this year. The rest of this piece is the corners the average paints over: five fronts, one at a time, and which one is actually on your menu.
Front one: why beef is expensive in twenty twenty-six, and why it isn’t the tariffs.

Beef is the domestic cattle cycle, not tariffs, not weather, and it is the one genuinely structural front in the whole storm. If you run beef, this is the line doing the most damage to your plate cost this year, and it is the exception that proves the rule about the spread: a real, multi-year squeeze hiding under a calm menu average.

The number that matters isn’t a price, it’s a headcount. The US cattle herd on January 1, twenty twenty-six was 86.2 million head, the smallest since 1951, a 75-year low. Beef cows came in at 27.6 million, down another 1%. Years of drought and high feed costs pushed ranchers to sell down their breeding stock, and you cannot rebuild a herd in a quarter. Retail beef ran 12.9% higher than a year earlier in May twenty twenty-six, though it slipped 1.3% month-on-month, still expensive, no longer accelerating. The level is high; the momentum is cooling.

Now the honest part, because even the structural front comes with a forecast, and forecasts wobble. Usda’s twenty twenty-six call for beef and veal is about +7.5%, inside a wide band of 3.1% to 12.2%, and that call was revised down from roughly 12.1% a month earlier. Read the herd count as the signal and the forecast percent as the noise around it. The signal says tight; the noise says nobody knows the exact number.

A five-step flow showing why beef relief is years away. Step one: the herd sits at eighty-six point two million head, the smallest since nineteen fifty-one, with beef cows down one percent. Step two: ranchers hold back heifers to rebuild breeding stock instead of selling them. Step three: that tightens the supply of cattle to slaughter now, so prices stay high before they loosen. Step four: a heifer retained today does not reach beef production until late twenty twenty-eight or later. Step five, the verdict: the price peak most likely lands in twenty twenty-seven, not this year, and this is a domestic supply story, not tariffs or weather.

The operator move on beef is the opposite of patience. Public wholesale quotes never arrive as your delivered price, so watch your own food-cost percentage on the beef plates line by line. If beef is a top-three cost on a plate, reprice it deliberately, on this year’s reality, not seasonally on a hunch that it’ll pass. It won’t pass in twenty twenty-six.
Front two: why coffee ran hot, then cooled.

Not everything is on fire, and the honest read has to hold the relief as firmly as the pain. Two fronts, coffee and insurance, are measured relief right now, and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of dishonesty.

Coffee ran genuinely hot early in the year. April twenty twenty-six had coffee up 18.5% over twelve months, with roasted at 17.3% and instant at 22.8%. Then it turned. By June, coffee fell 2.0% for the month and the broader non-alcoholic beverage index was up 2.9% year-on-year, still positive, no longer climbing. The honest phrase is “still expensive, no longer accelerating,” the same shape as beef but bending the friendlier way.

A trend line tracing coffee through twenty twenty-six to show a spike that eased but has not settled. In April, coffee's consumer price index was up eighteen and a half percent over the year, the peak. By June it had cooled, down two percent for the month. Arabica futures fell to around two dollars seventy a pound in late June. Then in mid-July the futures twitched back up to roughly three dollars thirty to three dollars fifty a pound on Brazil crop uncertainty. The takeaway is that coffee is the clearest easing front and also the least finished: down at the retail counter, but still jumpy on the futures board.

The cause underneath is worth stating plainly, because it’s a correlation, not a single villain. Coffee is high because of a real Brazil arabica shortfall, the twenty twenty-five/26 crop fell about 13% on bad weather, layered on top of a July twenty twenty-five tariff that cut Brazilian shipments to the US by more than half. Both are easing: a record Brazil crop is forecast for twenty twenty-six/27, and the tariff picture changed (more on that next). Usda’s twenty twenty-six forecast for non-alcoholic beverages is still +5.7%, above the menu blend, so “easing” is not the same as “cheap.” If coffee is a signature pour, hold your price, don’t lock a permanent number on an input this jumpy.

Insurance is the second, quieter relief. After years of steep renewals, commercial property premiums are forecast to rise only about 3, 4% in twenty twenty-six as that market softens. The exception is liquor liability, up as much as 20% in some markets, so a bar-heavy concept doesn’t get to bank the same relief a bakery does. More than eight in ten operators still name energy and card fees as strain. Relief in twenty twenty-six is real, and it is uneven, you can bank the coffee cool-down, but not evenly across every concept.
Front three: how tariffs actually hit restaurant costs in twenty twenty-six.

Tariffs did more damage in the headline than on most of my invoices, and the honest version splits perception from the line item cleanly. In the Nra’s twenty twenty-six survey, 68% of operators said tariffs contributed to higher food and beverage costs. That is a reported perception, not a measured amount, it tells you how the year felt , not that tariffs added a specific percentage to any plate. Never let a vendor turn that 68% into “tariffs added X% to your cost.”

The measured reality moves in two directions at once. The average effective US tariff rate was about 8.9% in April twenty twenty-six, down from a 16.5% peak after the Supreme Court struck the broadest tariffs, but still the highest since the 1970s. On the up-line: a Section 232 order kept a 50% tariff on steel, aluminum and copper, with 25% on derivative goods, effective June 8, twenty twenty-six, and that is the to-go-lid line from the top of this piece, plus cans, kegs, and a chunk of kitchen equipment. On the down-line: the 40% tariff on Brazilian coffee, beef, cocoa and fruit came off in November twenty twenty-five. One arrow moved packaging up; another moved coffee down, in the same year.
Tariffs did more damage in the headline than on most of my invoices. One line went up, another came down, same year.

Here is why every point still stings even when the arrow is small: restaurant food costs are already up about 34% against pre-pandemic levels, so you’re taking each new tariff on top of a base that never came back down. The move isn’t to fear the word “tariff”, it’s to ask your rep which Sku, in which direction. If it’s a can, a lid, or a piece of equipment, that’s a real tariff line you can plan around. If it’s coffee, the tariff went the other way.
Front four: the labor and staffing squeeze underneath every plate.

Labor isn’t a front beside the others, it’s the floor under all of them, and I’ll handle every number here as reported and cited, with no claim about policy or cause. Wages set the base cost of making anything on your menu, so when they move, they move with your food cost inside your prime cost .

The backdrop first. Private-sector wages rose 3.5% over the year to June twenty twenty-six, to an average of 37.64 dollars an hour; front-line food-service work sits far below that, with a median near 14.92 dollars. And the job market is cooling, not booming, leisure and hospitality shed about 61,000 jobs in June twenty twenty-six. A softer hiring market would normally take pressure off wages.

Except the applicant pool is thinning at the same time, and that is the part specific to this year. Foreign-born workers are about 22% of the restaurant workforce and a much larger share of the kitchen, 43 to 46% of chefs, roughly one in three of all chefs and cooks, per industry-association tallies of Census data. Over March to July twenty twenty-five, an estimated 137,000 immigrant restaurant workers left the workforce, part of about 1.7 million foreign-born workers, a 5% drop, leaving the US labor force in that window. A cooling job market and a thinning kitchen bench, landing on the same schedule, is why the labor line stays firm even as hiring slows. Those figures are reported staffing counts, cited below; the point here is only what they do to your cost of a shift.
Front five: why credit-card swipe fees are a top-three restaurant expense.

The quietest front is the one that grew the most while everyone watched food and labor: card swipe fees. US merchants paid a record 198.25 dollars billion in swipe fees in twenty twenty-five, up from 187.2 dollars billion in twenty twenty-four, with the credit-card portion alone at 157.8 dollars billion. The Nra ranks card processing as the third-largest operating expense for a majority of restaurants, behind only food and labor, and it has climbed more than 80% since the pandemic. Two in three operators say their fees rose in the past two years.

The reason it only ever ratchets is structural. The average Visa and Mastercard credit interchange rate, the biggest slice of a swipe fee, reached 2.36% of a purchase in twenty twenty-five, up from 2.02% in twenty ten. It behaves like a commission on every sale you make, food and tip and tax alike, and it compounds as your prices rise: raise the check to cover beef, and the swipe fee on that check goes up too.

A bar chart showing the average credit-card interchange, the biggest slice of a swipe fee, that a restaurant pays per one hundred dollars of card sales, tracing a line that only ratchets up. In twenty ten it was two dollars and two cents per hundred, an interchange rate of about two percent. By twenty twenty-five it had climbed to two dollars and thirty-six cents per hundred, now the third-largest operating expense behind food and labor. A thirty-eight billion dollar settlement approved in twenty twenty-six would trim it about ten basis points for five years, to roughly two dollars and twenty-six cents per hundred. The takeaway is that the settlement is real relief but a trim, not a reversal, against fifteen years of climbing.

Relief is coming, and it is partial. A 38 dollars billion Visa and Mastercard settlement won preliminary approval in June twenty twenty-six; it would trim the average interchange rate about 10 basis points for five years across more than 12 million merchants. Ten basis points against a 2.36% base is a trim, not a rescue, the earlier, larger deal was thrown out in twenty twenty-four as too small to matter. Meanwhile roughly a third of merchants now add a surcharge, up from one in five two years ago. Read this line every month the way you read food cost, and model the surcharge-versus-absorb question deliberately, because it trades a fee against your guest’s goodwill.
How restaurants are actually responding to higher costs.

The evidence on what operators do is clear, and it carries a warning inside it. Of the 82% who paid more for food in twenty twenty-five, the National Restaurant Association found the most common move wasn’t the menu price, it was the phone call to the supplier. 55% renegotiated with existing suppliers, 47% cut costs elsewhere, 43% adjusted portion sizes, 37% tightened waste tracking, and 31% substituted lower-cost ingredients. The operators who moved first mostly moved on cost, not on price.

A bar chart of how operators with higher food costs responded in twenty twenty-six, ranked. Eighty-two percent had higher food costs to begin with. Of those, fifty-five percent renegotiated with existing suppliers, the most common move. Forty-seven percent cut costs elsewhere in the operation. Forty-three percent adjusted portion sizes. Thirty-seven percent tracked food waste more closely. And thirty-one percent substituted lower-cost items on the menu. Separately, seventy-one percent plan to raise menu prices in twenty twenty-six, up from fifty-seven percent a year earlier. The ranking shows the field reaching for supplier and operational fixes first, and the price hike as one lever among several.

Here is the warning. The field’s default forward move is the price hike, 71% plan one this year, up from 57%, and the field’s central problem is that traffic already softened for about 60% of operators. Raising the check while the guest count falls is exactly the trap the tame average sets. Portion, mix, waste and supplier terms move margin without spending the contribution margin you get from a full room. Benchmark what you pay against the market before you touch the menu, Muntin’s free Vendor Benchmark is built for exactly that conversation with a rep.
How to read your own invoices instead of the headline.

The average is not your menu, and it is certainly not your P&L. So the close is a method, not a mood. Pull your top-five plate costs, and mark each front’s real direction against them: beef structural and rising through twenty twenty-seven, coffee cooling but jumpy, packaging and equipment up on Section 232, card fees up-then-trimmed, labor firm. Weight those by your menu mix, not the government’s basket, and the storm resolves into a short list of things that actually touch your plates.

A decision tree for sorting the cost storm onto your own menu. Start with your biggest-moving line item. If beef is a top-three plate cost, the verdict is structural: the cattle cycle peaks in twenty twenty-seven and relief is years out, so reprice deliberately, not seasonally. If coffee is a signature pour, hold: retail is cooling but futures spiked, so do not lock a permanent price on a moving input. If cards carry most of your sales, that is a structural third-largest expense and the settlement only trims about ten basis points, so model surcharge versus absorb. And if you import coffee, cocoa, or fruit, the Brazil forty-percent duty came off in November twenty twenty-five, which is a cost cut worth re-checking on your landed price.

What isn’t on the Cpi table is your own paperwork, and that is the only weather report that pays my rent. Read the weekly Cost Index against each ingredient’s own baseline window; price the plate in front of you against today’s invoice with plate-cost ; run the margin math before you set a new number; and watch the cost pulse week over week so a line like the to-go lids never sneaks up on you again. The storm was never one wind. It was five, at five speeds, and the only forecast that ever changed a price on my menu was the one printed on my own invoices.
Frequently asked questions.

How much have restaurant prices gone up in twenty twenty-six? Restaurant menu prices, what the government calls food away from home, rose 3.4% over the 12 months ending June twenty twenty-six, with full-service at 3.7% and fast food at 3.1%. That’s the tamest menu inflation in years, and Usda’s outlook has restaurants rising about 3.6% for the year against grocery’s 2.8%. The catch: the calm average hides much faster-moving lines underneath, like retail beef at 12.9% year-on-year.

Why are so many restaurants not profitable in twenty twenty-six? In the National Restaurant Association’s twenty twenty-six read, 42% of operators said their restaurant wasn’t profitable last year, and about 60% reported softer customer traffic even as sales dollars grew, revenue carried by higher checks, not more guests. With more than nine in ten operators naming food, labor, insurance, energy and swipe fees as significant challenges at once, the squeeze is on the whole P&L, not one line.

Why is beef so expensive for restaurants in twenty twenty-six? Beef is a domestic cattle-cycle story, not tariffs or weather. The US cattle herd on January 1, twenty twenty-six was 86.2 million head, the smallest since 1951, after years of drought and herd liquidation. Retail beef ran 12.9% higher year-on-year in May twenty twenty-six, and Usda forecasts twenty twenty-six beef and veal up about 7.5% (within a wide 3.1, 12.2% band). Because rebuilding a herd takes years, the price peak most likely lands in twenty twenty-seven, not this year.

Are tariffs raising restaurant food costs in twenty twenty-six? In part, and unevenly. 68% of operators said tariffs contributed to higher food and beverage costs, but that’s a reported perception, not a measured amount. The measured picture moves both ways: a Section 232 order kept 50% tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper effective June 8, twenty twenty-six, raising cans, lids and equipment, while the 40% tariff on Brazilian coffee, beef and fruit came off in November twenty twenty-five. Ask which Sku and which direction before accepting a tariff surcharge.

Did coffee prices go down in twenty twenty-six? They cooled. Coffee ran hot early in the year, up 18.5% year-on-year in April twenty twenty-six, then turned, falling 2.0% month-on-month in June, with the broader non-alcoholic beverage index up 2.9% year-on-year. Arabica futures dropped to about 2.70 dollars a pound in late June before rebounding to roughly 3.30 dollars, 3.50 in mid-July. So retail coffee is easing but not settled, and Usda still forecasts non-alcoholic beverages up 5.7% for the year.

Why are credit card swipe fees such a big restaurant expense in twenty twenty-six? US merchants paid a record 198.25 dollars billion in card swipe fees in twenty twenty-five, and the Nra ranks card processing as the third-largest operating expense for a majority of restaurants, behind food and labor, up more than 80% since the pandemic. The average credit interchange rate reached 2.36% of a purchase in twenty twenty-five, up from 2.02% in twenty ten, and it compounds as prices rise. A 38 dollars billion Visa and Mastercard settlement won preliminary approval in June twenty twenty-six but trims only about 10 basis points for five years, real relief, not a reversal.

What can restaurants do about rising costs in twenty twenty-six? Of operators with higher food costs, the most common move wasn’t the menu price, it was the supplier call: 55% renegotiated with existing suppliers, 47% cut costs elsewhere, 43% adjusted portion sizes, 37% tightened waste tracking, and 31% substituted lower-cost items. 71% plan to raise prices this year, but raising checks into softer traffic is the trap the tame average sets. Sort each front onto your own menu, benchmark what you pay before you reprice, and read your own invoices against the Cost Index and plate-cost, not the headline.

Every number here carries its source in the drawers above, the Bls Consumer Price Index, Usda Ers and Nass, the National Restaurant Association’s twenty twenty-six State of the Industry, the Nilson Report and court filings on swipe fees, and the Tax Foundation and Federal Register on tariffs. This is a read of public data as of July 16, twenty twenty-six, not a forecast of your costs. Check my math.
Key takeaways
Don’t reprice off the 3.4% headline: the average is the tamest in years, but 42% of operators still didn’t profit and traffic softened for about 60%. The pain is in the spread, not the mean.
Beef is the one structural front, a 75-year-low cattle herd, a twenty twenty-seven peak. If it’s a top-three plate cost, reprice deliberately; “wait it out” loses money through twenty twenty-seven.

Bank the easing fronts without over-repricing: coffee cooled 2.0% in June, the Brazil tariff on coffee and beef came off, a 38 dollars billion swipe-fee settlement trims interchange, and property insurance is softening.

Watch the quiet lines: card swipe fees hit a record 198.25 dollars billion in twenty twenty-five and are the third-largest expense; packaging and equipment are up on Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs.
Sort every front onto your own menu, then read your invoices against the Cost Index and plate-cost, the only forecast that changes a price is the one printed on your own paperwork.
